title: Rowan and the Moonberry Mix-Up
markdown:
Young Rowan was a wizard with a gift for magic, though his spells sometimes had a mind of their own. His days were spent among bubbling potions and old scrolls, with only Hops, his mountain hare, for company. Hops was a creature of comfort: nibbling clover and, most importantly, sleeping. White fur as soft as a freshly fallen cloud, long twitchy ears often drooping in slumber. A true master of the nap.

One crisp morning, dawn painting the peaks rose and gold, Rowan discovered a strange problem. His prize moonberries, plump and shimmering with captured moonlight, were missing from their enchanted basket. In their place: a pile of ordinary very red cherries. The market in the village below opened with the sun, and he had promised Elder Meadowsweet the moonberries for her famous twilight tarts. A tremor in his chest. His magic felt tied to forgetfulness. Hands clumsy. Parchment blurring. He knew, with sinking certainty, that he had accidentally swapped his moonberry basket with Farmer Giles’ cherry basket. He pictured Elder Meadowsweet’s disappointed face. His heart felt as heavy as a wet wool sock.

“Hops, we must venture forth. A great misunderstanding awaits correction before the market bells ring. Elder Meadowsweet’s tarts depend on us.”

Hops, nestled in a sunbeam, twitched a whisker. Blinked slowly, as if waking were monumental. Then, with a soft sigh that ruffled his fur, he settled deeper into his nap. Rowan scooped him up, careful not to disturb. Soft warmth against his chest.

The forest floor was a carpet of pine needles, sharp and sweet, damp earth. Find Farmer Giles. Explain the swap. Retrieve the berries before the sun climbed too high.

Deeper in, a faint high-pitched chink-chink-chink. Tiny bells tapped by a very small hammer. The air shimmered, hint of damp moss. Hops snuffled, a puff of warm air against Rowan’s chin.

“What is that peculiar sound? As if someone is trying to polish a pebble with a sigh. Or a tiny knight practising swordplay with a teacup.”

The sound led them off the well-worn path to a sun-dappled clearing. In the centre sat a tiny dragon, no bigger than a plump robin, scales shimmering with the colours of a rainbow after a spring shower. Pepplewing, known for a quiet nature and a love of all things sparkly. The chink was his tiny sharp claws on a large rough-hewn stone, trying to coax a gleam from its dull surface.

“Hello there, little one.” Hops still asleep. Pepplewing startled, puffing iridescent smoke that smelled of warm honey. Wide golden eyes like two drops of sunshine.

“You are a tiny dragon. And what a beautiful stone, though it seems a little shy about showing its sparkle.” Rowan set Hops beside a mossy log. The hare curled tighter, ears flopping over his nose.

“I am trying to make this stone shine like the moon,” Pepplewing squeaked, voice like dry autumn leaves. “But it is so heavy. And my claws are just too small.” He nudged; it barely budged, stubbornly dull.

Rowan felt a familiar tingle in his fingertips. He could cast levitation, or a might-enhancement, and have the stone moving in a flash. Quicker. Then he remembered the moonberries, the cherries, the ticking market. He almost asked if the dragon had seen Farmer Giles—easy magic of someone else’s memory. He stopped. He needed to remember and explain his own mistake.

As he spoke that intention, Hops stirred. A magnificent arch of fluffy white, a shake of head, a sudden wide-eyed blink that took in the whole clearing. Fully awake. He hopped closer, nose twitching toward Pepplewing and the stubborn stone. Dragon and ancient rock had finally broken through his slumber.

Pepplewing listened, rainbow scales dimming slightly. He stopped pecking. “Moonberries? The ones that glow softly, like little captured moons, and taste like starlight and dew?”

“They are.”

“Ah.” New energy. He hopped onto the stone. “Perhaps if you roll the stone, not lift it? Rolling makes things easier than lifting, like a log rather than carrying it. And when you speak to Farmer Giles, tell him the sound of the cherries made you think of the glow of the moonberries. Sometimes sounds and lights get mixed up in our heads, just like baskets. My own mum once mistook a glow-worm for a fallen star.”

The sound of the cherries. The glow of the moonberries. A simple perfect idea, a hidden key. Rowan looked at his now-awake hare, nudging Pepplewing’s tail, and the tiny dragon who had offered unexpected wisdom. A wizard, a hare, and a miniature dragon, contemplating a stubbornly dull stone.

“Thank you. That is truly splendid advice. Almost as good as finding a lost sock.” He scooped Hops back. “We have a market to reach, and a misunderstanding to mend.”

They hurried through pine and damp earth, a faint hint of honey from dragon breath. A lightness in Rowan’s step more satisfying than any grand spell.

They burst into the bustling square: vendors, fresh bread, ripe fruit. Elder Meadowsweet, brow furrowed, speaking to Farmer Giles. Rowan rushed to her, Hops peeking, ears twitching. He explained everything, voice clear and steady. Cherries. The sound that reminded him of moonlight. Pepplewing’s clever idea. Elder Meadowsweet’s eyes widened, then crinkled with amusement.

“You wizards. Always lost in thought, or in your baskets. But your moonberries are indeed here, safe with Farmer Giles. He was wondering where his cherries had gone. Quite peculiar, so red and round, unlike his usual speckled ones.”

Rowan’s heart swelled with relief and a quiet understanding. He noticed Farmer Giles about to walk away without his cherries. “Wait.” He gathered the red cherries. “Perhaps you could trade these for the moonberries. They might not be your usual, but they are quite sweet.” Giles’s face broke into a wide grin. Baskets exchanged.

As Rowan turned to leave he nearly left his spellbook on a stall. He caught it with a confident smile. Almost a muddle. Not today. Hops, nestled contentedly, was already beginning to doze, a soft peaceful rumble from his fluffy chest. The market went on selling bread. The tarts would have moonlight in them after all.
characters: Rowan (young wizard whose spells have a mind of their own), Hops (a mountain hare who masters the nap)
